Graduate and Research Programs.

Graduate study and research may be pursued in the areas of Mass and Heat Transfer, Reaction Kinetics and Catalysis, Transport Phenomena, Thermodynamics, Process Dynamics and Control, and Computational Methods in Chemical Engineering.

Examples from the current research programme are Heat and Mass Transfer from spheres and other shapes under combined natural and forced convection; Turbulent heat transfer and studies on the transition of the boundary layer; Fluid mechanics and heat transfer studies in solid-gas systems; Heat transfer with chemical reactions; Thermal radiation to porous surfaces with thin liquid films; Unit operations with coupled heat and mass transport such as spray drying; Application of monomolecular films to evaporation reduction; Dye catalyzed photoxidation with the objective of application to photo-electrochemical cells; Mechanisms of catalyzed reactions in solution; Investigation of the rate determining steps in complex heterogeneous reactions; Studies of the contribution of surface diffusion in catalysis; Models for the pyrolysis of hydrocarbons and petroleum fractions; Effectiveness factors for complex reactions; Chemical process systems theory with particular emphasis on the identification and optimal prediction problem related to non-stationary systems.

Graduate and Research Programmes

Both co-operative and conventional graduate study in Civil Engineering can be undertaken, leading to the degrees of Master of Applied Science or Doctor of Philosophy. There are at present four major areas of study in which specialization may be undertaken: Structural Engineering, Geotechnical Engineering, Water Resources Engineering and Transportation Engineering.

Structural Engineering (Ariaratnam, Cohn, Lind, Poorooshasb, Sherbourne, Topper and Wright.) Laboratory facilities include a structural models laboratory, a concrete laboratory, a properties of materials laboratory, and a large structural engineering laboratory equipped with a 100,000 Ibs. Losenhausen universal testing machine. A major study in this area is Theoretical and Applied Mechanics. Among the courses of study are CE 609 to 620. In addition, students may choose from a variety of appropriate courses in mathematics, physics and mechanical engineering.

Current research in structural engineering and applied mechanics include studies in non-linear vibrations, plastic instability of structures, lateral reinforcement and column ductility in reinforced concrete, model testing in soil mechanics, plasticity and instability in plates and in shell structures, behaviour of metal structures under cyclic loadings of low frequency, large deflection studies of shells and membranes, plastic strain and energy in fatigue, theory of design and safety of structures, inelastic behaviour of framed and shell structures, analysis of latticed space structures, ultimate load studies in reinforced concrete, elastic-plastic strength of pressure vessels, and studies of plastic wave propagation.

Geotechnical Engineering (Karrow, Poorooshasb, Scott and White.) Major subdivisions of study in this area are Soil Mechanics, Foundation Engineering and Engineering Geology. Appropriate courses of study are CE 611, 614, 651 to 654, and 698. The Department has two fully equipped soil mechanics and foundation engineering laboratories...

Current research activities are investigations into the yield behaviour of soils, earth pressure studies, foundation settlement research and model testing in soils, pleistocene geology of southern Ontario areas, and studies of stresses in earth dams.
Department of Civil Engineering

Water Resources Engineering (Dryan, Fisher) Included under this area are studies in Environmental Health Engineering. At the present time there are two laboratories, one of which is equipped for most standard physical, chemical and biological analyses of water and waste water. The second laboratory is reserved for graduate students’ projects and research studies. This laboratory is furnished with specialized equipment built for unit process studies and advanced specialized studies in environmental health. Courses in this area are Biology 31 and 601, CE 671 to 675, 681 and 698.

Transportation Engineering (McLaughlin and Hutchinson) Major subdivisions of study are Highway Engineering, Traffic Engineering and Urban Planning. Appropriate courses of study are CE 640 to 643 and 698. Supplementary courses in urban and area planning may be taken from the Department of Geography.

courses.label: CIVE 609
courses.title: Advanced Theory of Structures
paras: Numerical methods in structural analysis. Advanced problems in stability of frames, trusses and their components. Dynamic loadings and shock effects. Vibrations.
One term.

courses.label: CIVE 610
courses.title: Inelastic Behaviour of Ductile Members and Structures
paras: Effect of inelastic strains in structural members. Simple plastic theory and limit design of plane frames, grids, plates, and arch structures. Deflections. Shakedown. Inelastic instability and the influence of strain hardening. Dynamic loading. Introduction to general theory of plasticity.
One term.

courses.label: CIVE 611
courses.title: Elementary Mechanics of Continua
paras: A general introduction to the mechanics of solids and fluids. Stress, deformation and flow. Materials and their rheological properties. The equations of elastic solids; problems in linear elasticity. Equations of fluid mechanics. Problems in viscous and ideal fluid flow. Yield criteria; the flow rule. Simple problems in plasticity and theoretical soil mechanics.
One term.

courses.label: CIVE 612
courses.title: Experimental Mechanics
paras: Classification and estimation of errors. Smoothing of experimental data. Similitude and model laws. Simulation of frames, trusses, plates and shells. Analogue methods in experimental stress analysis. Electrical and mechanical strain gauges, transducers. Brittle coatings. Photoelasticity.
One term.

courses.label: CIVE 614
courses.title: Mechanics of Continua I
paras: A _ unified rigorous introduction to the mechanics of solids and fluids. Geometrical preliminaries, introduction to tensors, tensor fields, integral theorems. Analysis of stress, deformation and rate of deformation. Energy and Entropy. Fundamental laws, conservation of mass, momentum and energy. Simple constitutive equations.
Normally, this course would be studied for credit only by students intending to register for CE 615 in a subsequent term. One term.

courses.label: CIVE 615
courses.title: Mechanics of Continua If Application of the fundamental principles of mechanics to formulate and solve problems in the mechanics of ideal and viscous fluids, elastic and plastic solids and materials with time-dependent mechanical properties. Electroelasticity
paras: Prerequisite: CE 614 or CE 611.
One term.

courses.label: CIVE 616
courses.title: Seminar in Mechanics of Continua
paras: Further individual study of selected topics in the mechanics of continuous media. Presentation of progress and discussion of reports in seminar form.
Prerequisite: CE 614.
One term.

courses.label: CIVE 617
courses.title: Elasticity
paras: Analysis of stress and strain. Stress-strain relations. Boundaryvalue formulation. Strain energy, variational principles. Theories of plane strain, plane stress and generalized plane stress of torsion and of flexure. Three-dimensional elastostatic problems, stress function representation. Elastic waves. Approximate methods.
One term.

courses.label: CIVE 618
courses.title: Plasticity
paras: Foundations of the continuum theory of plasticity. Yield criteria and associated flow rules. Fundamental equations. Variational principles; uniqueness. Limit analysis. Plane strain. Torsion. Spherical and axisymmetric problems. Applications to problems of strength analysis and forming processes. Plastic instability.
Prerequisite: CE 611 or CE 614.
One term.

courses.label: CIVE 619
courses.title: Theory of Plates and Shells
paras: Differential geometry of surfaces. Equations of equilibrium and deformation in orthogonal curvilinear co-ordinates. Momentless theory of shells. Energy formulations and stability problems in shells. Limit analysis.

courses.label: CIVE 620
courses.title: Theories of Design
paras: The problem of rational design. Fundamental philosophies in general design of engineering systems. Morphology of the design process. Nature of design data. Design of transportation systems and structures. Structural synthesis approach. Evaluative functions. Utility theory. Hierarchial systems of objectives. Sub-optimization. Design against risk and uncertainty in resistive systems. Design against noise in communication systems. One term.

EE 12. Electricity and Magnetism I. An introductory course in electricity and magnetism.

(a) - Electrostatics - Coulomb’s Law, the electrostatic field, Guass’ Law. Electric potential and the equations of Laplace and Poisson. Capacitance, stored energy in a capacitor. Polarization properties of dielectrics, displacement, boundary conditions. D.C. circuits, current and resistance, electromotive force, Ohm’s Law, Kirchoff’s Laws. The potentiometer and wheatstone bridge.

(b) - Magnetostatics - The Biot-Savart Law, the magnetic induction field, Amperes Law, solenoids. Torque on a current carrying loop, the galvanometer. Magnetic force on moving charges, the d.c. motor.
EE 13. Electricity and Magnetism II. A second course in electricity and magnetism containing an introduction to time-varying fields.

Electromagnetic induction - Faraday’s Law, Lenz’s Law, motional emf. Mutual and self inductance, stored magnetic energy. Elementary motors and generators. Magnetism in matter - magnetic susceptibility and permeability, the magnetic field, boundary conditions. Ferromagnetism, hysteresis, magnetic curcuits. Alternating current circuits - complex notation, phasor diagrams. Electronics - diode and triode vacuum tubes and applications. Maxwell’s equations and electromagnetic waves - displacement current, the equation of continuity, one-dimensional electromagnetic waves, Poynting vector dipole antennas, refraction at a boundary, waveguides.

EE 23. Analogue Computation. Principles of continuous computation, computing elements, computer diagrams, programming and scaling. Solution of linear and nonlinear differential equations, transfer function and system simulation, signal-flow graphs and state-equations, elgebraic models. Partial differential equations, iteration techniques, design aspects, hybrid systems. Prerequisite: Math 31, Math 45.
3 lectures, alternate laboratory, one term.

EE 24. Logic and Switching I. The logical design of relay and electronic switching circuits. Boolean algebra. Algebraic equivalent of switching logic; tables of combinations. Relay contact networks, elementary diode, vacuum tube, transistor, and magnetic core switching circuits.
Prerequisite: EE 42, EE 52.
3 lectures, one term.

EE 25. Logic and Switching II. A course in engineering principles of stored programme digital computers. Design of arithmetic section, coding, control. Over-all logical organization and memory techniques.

Graduate and Research Programmes
Graduate Credit in Electrical Engineering

Graduate credit is measured in “units”. A unit is a course at the graduate level taken for one semester, and which requires, as a prerequisite, preparation at the Bachelor’s level. Two units are given to a graduate course which continues for two semesters. Senior undergraduate courses as approvel by the Electrical Engineering Department may be allowed as credit for graduate students at one-half unit per semester. For each student, no more than two units total credit can be given to undergraduate courses.

A thesis is not required, but if submitted and accepted, will count either four or five units credit under EE 699. Thesis topics are worked out in discussions between students and faculty. No more than two units will be credited to a student taking EE 698. Furthermore, it is not possible to obtain credit under both EE 698 and EE 699.

Students transferring from other universities of recognized standing may be allowed a maximum of two units for graduate courses previously taken. No credit is given for any undergraduate course taken at other universities.

A full-time student is permitted to take a maximum load of five units for a semester. For part-time student, the maximum load is reduced from five units per semester by one unit for each seven hours per week of employment or outside work.
The Master’s Degree Programme
The Master’s degree programme in Electrical Engineering is designed to be flexible, and to accommodate regular full-time and part-time students, and cooperative graduate students from industry.
A complete programme consists of a total of ten units. Each student’s programme must be approved by the Electrical Engineering Department, and is worked out with a professor who acts as an advisor.

The student’s course work is considered unsatisfactory, and he is required to discontinue, if more than one course in Electrical Engineering receives grade below 66%, or more than two courses in other fields than Electrical Engineering receives grade below 66%.
Department of Electrical Engineering

A thesis student must be registered in EE 699 continuously without interruption, and the thesis must be done under the direct supervision of a professor of the Electrical Engineering Department, and is finally approved and accepted by that professor.

All course work and thesis for Master’s degree must be completed within four consecutive academic years. It is possible for a full-time student of exceptional ability to complete the requirements for the Master’s degree in two semesters, or one academic year.
The Ph.D. Programme

The major objective of the Ph.D. programme is to emphasize the importance of performing original research of high calibre. The requirements of the comprehensive examination, the supervising committee, course work, and the language examination, are all considered as aids to performing satisfactory research. Facilities for Ph.D. programmes are available in most fields of study described under Research.

English Major in General Arts

In Year I the prospective English major should select English 100, Philosophy 100, Science 100, at least one of French 100, German 100, and Latin 100, and other subjects in accord with the general regulations.

In Year II the English major shall complete English 200 and 250; in the course of Years II and III he shall complete one further Honours English course and at least two of English 210, 220, 225, 230, 300, 335, or any Honours English courses; in Year III he shall also complete English 345 and shall write a Comprehensive Examination in the general field of English Literature.

Subjects related to the study of English, and from which the English major is expected to choose his optional courses, are the following: Classics, French, German, Hisotry (especially English or American), Philosophy, Psychology, Religious Knowledge, Russian, Sociology and Spanish.

Note on numbering: English 100 and 200 are designed for both Honours and General students. Otherwise courses numbered 250-299, 350-399, and 450-499 are Honours courses, and all others are General courses.

Note on prerequisites: Normally English 100 (or its equivalent at another University) will be prerequisite to all courses numbered 200 and above (except 225 and 235). In addition English 200 (or its equivalent) will normally be prerequisite to English 380, 450, 455, 460 and 470.

courses.label: GEOG 15
courses.title: Survey of Geography
paras: This one term course presents a general review of the field of geography, its scope, approach, and basic concepts. The primary aim is to provide the student with background, material, readings, sources and ideas against which major political developments, international economic relationships, and current problems of the commonwealth and underdeveloped areas may be viewed. Course topics include: the development and character of modern geography; fundamentals of physiography; population patterns and problems; resources, economic growth and industrialization; the geographic bases of political patterns and events; and urban growth and land use planning.
3 lectures, half course.

courses.label: GEOG 100
courses.title: Introductory Physical and Cultural Geography
paras: This course is designed to introduce the student to the field of modern geography, its methods, concepts, materials and point of view. A major part of the course is devoted to a systematic examination of the elements of the natural environment, (including landforms, weather, and climate), and their distribution and significance in the human habitat. Selected aspects of economic and political geography are then considered, with an emphasis on world resources and the geographic bases of economic development, international trade, and political relationships. Note: Geography 100, or its equivalent, is normally a prerequisite for other courses in geography.
2 lectures, 2 hours laboratory.

courses.label: GEOG 200
courses.title: Climatology and Meteorology
paras: Advanced study of the elements of climate and weather. Analysis of world climatic and weather patterns. Effects of climate on man’s activities and on distribution of natural vegetation and soils. Weather forecasting. Applied climatology.
2 lectures, 2 hours laboratory. (Half course, given in fall term).

courses.label: GEOG 220
courses.title: World Regional Geography
paras: A survey of the major natural and political regions of the world with attention to areas of current interest in world affairs; the interrelationships of physical, economic, and cultural factors, and their implications for problems of economic growth.
2 lectures, 2 hours seminar.

courses.label: GEOG 260

2 lectures, 2 hours laboratory.

courses.label: GEOG 310
courses.title: Geography ef World Resources and Industries
paras: An analysis of man’s economic activity; the nature and occurrence of resources, problems of resource development and conservation; world distribution of primary production, and structure of world trade; major industrial regions and locational factors affecting representative industries.
2 lectures, 2 hours seminar.

courses.label: GEOG 341

3 lectures.

2 lectures, 2 hours seminar.

paras: Principles of problem statement, analysis and concept creation. Discussions of the planning function, as applied to physical and economic feasibility, concept selection and project design. 3 hours lectures (including discussion and problem sessions) one term, first year.

courses.title: Introduction to Engineering Systems
paras: Introduction to basic methods of analysis through mathematical models for components and processes. Systematic formulation of terminal representations and of system equations for linear systems, utilizing terminal and system graph concepts in conjunction with matrix notation. Solutions through Laplace transforms and by computer methods. Examples are drawn from the various engineering disciplines.

Prerequisite: GE 21. 4 hours, one term.

Irreversible heat transfer, mechanisms, calculation of heat flow in simple practical applications.
3 hours lectures.

courses.label: GER 32
courses.title: Fluid Mechanics
paras: Basic concepts and laws of the statics, kinetmatics and dynamics of fluids. Continuity, energy and momentum equations, viscosity effects and their engineering applications. Introductory treatment of energy dissipation and boundary layer formation. Dimensional analysis and similarity laws.
Prerequisite: ME 12, Math 31.
3 hours lecture, 3 hours laboratory.

courses.label: GER 41

paras: An analytical treatment of statics and resistance of materials. Equilibrium of particles, rigid bodies and deformable bodies. Vector fields. Bar systems. Introduction to stress and strain. Stressstrain relationships. Elastic and inelastic behaviour of prismatic members subjected to axial, shearing, torsional and flexural deformations.
2 lectures, 2 hours tutorials, one term.

courses.label: GER 61
courses.title: History and Philosophy of Science
paras: The nature of science; science and technology in Egypt and Babylon. The development of science in Greece; the Orphic mysteries and the Ionian philosophers. Plato and Aristotle; Archimedes. The Alexandrian school and the separation of science and philosophy. Technology under the Roman Empire. The mediaeval attitude toward science. The Renaissance. Copernicus and Galileo. Sir Isaac Newton. The physical and biological sciences during the 18th century. Developments during the 19th Century in physics, chemistry, technology, geology, evolution, and the rise of modern genetics. The 20th century revolution in pure science and technology.
3 lectures.

Subject to departmental approval, one of the courses may be selected from graduate courses in another department. The candidate will also be required to have a reading knowledge of an appropriate second language.

In proceeding to the degree by courses and a thesis the candidate will offer: a) History 600, b) a minor field (a second graduate course) and c) a major field (a thesis and a comprehensive examination in the period). The candidate will also be required to have a reading knowledge of an appropriate second language.

courses.label: MATH 12
courses.title: Calculus I
paras: Functions and limits, the derivative. Differentiation formulae. Applications to tangents, rates, extrema. The indefinite and definite integrals, fundamental theorem of integral calculus. Applications to area, volume, centroids, moments of inertia, fluid pressure, work, potential. Introduction to the trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic functions. Transcendental functions. Parametric and polar equations. Formal integration and applications to physical problems. Students will work selected problems under supervision. A certain proportion of the problems will include mathematical formulation of physical problems.
3 lectures, 2 hours problems.

courses.label: MATH 21
courses.title: Algebra and Solid Geometry
paras: The rational, real, and complex number systems. Polynomial functions. Theory of equations. Determinants. Vector and matric notation. Co-ordinates in 3 dimensions. Systems of planes and lines. Standard equations of quadric surfaces. Spherical and cylindrical co-ordinates.
2 lectures, 1 hour problems.

courses.label: MATH 22
courses.title: Calculus I
paras: A continuation of course 12. Infinite series and power series. Partial derivatives. Multiple integration and applications to areas, volumes, centroids, moments. Introduction to differential equations.
Prerequisite: Math 12.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: MATH 23
courses.title: Numerical Methods
paras: Introduction to the use of desk calculators. Simple problems on interpolation, solution of algebraic equations, numerical evaluation of integrals, systems of equations.
2 hours problems, one term.

courses.label: MATH 24
courses.title: Mathematics Problems
paras: A problems course to accompany Math 22. 2 hours problems, one term.

courses.label: MATH 31
courses.title: Differential Equations
paras: Standard methods of solution. Applications to physical and engineering problems. Linear equations with constant co-efficients. Systems of differential equations. Solution by series. Numerical methods of solution. Partial differential equations; applications of partial differential equations.
Prerequisite: Math 22.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: MATH 32
courses.title: Numerical Analysis
paras: Ordinary, divided, and central difference interpolation formulae. Graphic and numerical solutions of algebraic and transcendental equations. Computation with series and integrals. Systems of linear equations. Determinants and matrices. Eigenvalue problems. Iterative procedures. Relaxation methods. Difference equations. Mathematical principles associated with electronic computers.
Prerequisite: Math 23.
2 lectures, 4 hours problems, one term.
Department of Mathematics

courses.label: MATH 33
courses.title: Differential Calculus
paras: Real numbers, sequences, limits, continuity. The derivative. General Theorem of Mean Value. Functions of several variables, implicit functions, Jacobians. Power series with complex terms, the Taylor series for functions of several variables, constrained extrema. The elementary functions for a complex variable.
Prerequisites: Math 22,31.
3 lectures, one term.

34, Integral Calculus. Systematic treatment of formal integration. Differential equations. Calculus of variations. Fourier series. Riemann integration, improper integrals, multiple integrals with applications. Line integrals, theorems of Green and Stokes.
Prerequisites: Math 22, 31.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: MATH 41
courses.title: Applied Analysis I
paras: Partial differentiation, Laplace transforms, special functions. Fourier series, second order differential equations. 3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: MATH 42
courses.title: Vector Methods
paras: Scalar and vector products; curl, divergence, and gradient. Use of vectors and matrices in discussion of physical problems in mechanics, fluid flow, and electromagnetism. Introduction to tensors. Prerequisites: Math 22, 31, and consent of instructor.
2 lectures, 1 hour problems, one term.
44, Complex Variable. Cauchy-Riemann equations, the Cauchy integral theorems, conformal mapping, the Taylor and Laurent series, contour integration. Prerequisites: Math 33, 34.
2 lectures, 1 hour problems, one term.

courses.label: MATH 45
courses.title: Applied Analysis II A continuance of some topics listed in Math 41, complex variables, calculus of variations
paras: 2 lectures, one term.

courses.label: MATH 51
courses.title: Probability and Statistics
paras: Frequency distributions; probability; Binomial, Normal, and Poisson laws. Sampling theory. Distribution of Chi-squared, F, and t. Hypothesis testing, quality control, regression theory. Curve fitting. Analysis of variance, introduction to experimental design.
Prerequisite: Math 22.
2 lectures, 3 hours problems, one term.

courses.label: MATH 53
courses.title: Operational Methods
paras: The Heaviside Calculus and the Laplace Transform. Admittance, impedance, and other operators. Applications of operator techniques to problems in electricity, mechanics, and heat.
Prerequisites: Math 22, 31, and consent of instructor.
2 lectures, 1 hour problems, one term.

courses.label: MATH 54
courses.title: Differential Equations of Mathematical Physics
paras: The wave equation. Potentials. Boundary-value problems. Eigenvalue problems. Expansions in series of orthogonal functions. Spherical, cylindrical, and ellipsoidal harmonics. Prerequisites: Math 22, 31, and consent of instructor.
2 lectures, one hour problems, one term.

courses.label: MATH 55
courses.title: Digital Computer Programming
paras: Fundamentals of digital computers, including memory types, arithmetic compononents, input-output and control units. Binary numbers, floating-point arithmetic, flow charting, machine-language coding. Automatic coding, including assemblers, compilers, and translators. Interpretive routines.
Prerequisite: Math 32. 3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: MATH 56
courses.title: Matrix Algebra
paras: Fundamental properties of vector spaces. Matrices as operators in vector spaces. Quadratic forms. Functions of matrices. Applications.
Prerequisite: Math 21.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: MATH 85
courses.title: Cartesian Co-ordinates
paras: The distance formula. Functions and their graphical representation. The linear function. Forms of the line equation. The quadratic function and roots of quadratic equations. Algebraic and geometric approach to loci. Standard forms for the circle, parabola, ellipse, hyperbola. The number system. Polynomial functions. Remainder theorem. Functions of more than one variable. Equations in one or more variables. The general trigonometric functions, their values and graphs. Radian measure. Compound angle formulae. Trigonometric formulae. Trigonometric equations. The sine and cosine laws for triangles. The logarithmic function. The laws of logarithms. Arithmetic and geometric series. The binomial series. Properties of the binomial coefficients. Permutations and combinations.
3 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 100
courses.title: Fundamental Concepts of Mathematics
paras: A terminal course designed for Arts students who wish to learn something of the fundamental ideas of mathematics but who will not be encountering technical problems of application. The course will include discussion of the fundamental concepts involved in a selection of topics chosen from mathematical areas such as Calculus, Statistics, Probability, Projective Geometry, Non-Euclidean Geometry, Set Theory, Group Theory, Field Theory, Boolean Algebra, Mathematical Logic, Vector Spaces, Matrices, Numerical Analysis.
3 lectures.
Department of Mathematics

paras: Functions and limits. The derivative. Differentiation of algebraic functions. Applications to tangents, rates, minima and maxima. Integration as the limit of a sum. Fundamental theorem of integral calculus with applications to areas, volumes, and moments. Power series. Partial differentiation.
3 lectures. .

courses.label: MATH 131
courses.title: Algebra and Solid Geometry
paras: The real and complex number systems. Polynomial functions. Theory of equations. Determinants. Vector and matrix notation. Elementary solid geometry, planes and lines, the standard quadric surfaces. Co-ordinate systems.
2 lectures, one hour problems.

courses.label: MATH 132
courses.title: Numerical Procedures
paras: Introduction to finite differences. Interpolation. Numerical integration. Introduction to the use of electric computers.
1 lecture, 2 hours problems.

courses.label: MATH 230

3 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 231
courses.title: Differential Calculus
paras: Real numbers, sequences. Limits. Continuity. Derivatives. Functions of several variables. Implicit functions. Jacobians. Taylor’s series with geometric applications. Power series with complex terms. The elementary functions for a complex variable.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 232
courses.title: Integral Calculus
paras: Methods of formal integration. Differential equations. Fourier series. Riemann integration and applications. Calculus of variations. Line integrals. Stokes’ and Green’s theorems.
3 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 233
courses.title: Probability and Statistics
paras: Frequency distributions. Probability. Binomial, Normal, and Poisson laws. Sampling theory. Curve fitting. Distributions of Chisquared, F, and t. Hypothesis testing. Quality control. Regression theory. Analysis of variance. Introduction to experimental design.
1 lecture, 2 hours problems.

courses.label: MATH 234
courses.title: Mechanics
paras: The theory of frames. Centres of gravity. Moments of inertia. Equilibrium conditions. Gravitational motion. The dynamics of rigid bodies.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 235
courses.title: Actuarial Mathematics
paras: The theory of compound interest and of life contingencies. An elementary course on the mathematics of investment and on applications of probability to problems of life and death. Annuities, single and annual premiums. Reserves. Standard actuarial notation.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 236
courses.title: Elementary differential Equations
paras: An introduction to first order differential equations. Applications to growth, decay, reactions. Linear equations with constant coefficients. Systems of equations; vector and matric methods. Solutions in series. Introduction to partial differential equations.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 330
courses.title: Euclidean and Projective Geometry
paras: The nine-points circle. The Simson line. Cross ratio. Projection. Harmonic ranges and involutions. Properties of circles. Axioms of incidence for projective geometry. Duality. Theorems of Pappus and Desargues. Introduction of co-ordinates. Conic sections. Introduction to non-Euclidean geometry.
3 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 332
courses.title: Theory of Functions

courses.label: MATH 333
courses.title: Differential Equations
paras: First-order differential equations. Linear equations with constant coefficients. Solutions in series. Systems of differential equations. Introduction to partial differential equations. Introduction to integral equations.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 334
courses.title: Numerical Methods
paras: Finite differences. Solution of equations. Computation with series and integrals. Linear systems and matric methods. Difference equations and relaxation methods. Numerical solution of partial differential equations. Methods employing electronic computers.
2 lectures, 2 hours laboratory.

courses.label: MATH 335
courses.title: Finite Differences
paras: A theoretical course in the calculus of finite differences to include summation, the differences of zero, numerical integration, the relation between integration and summation. An introduction to difference equations. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 336
courses.title: Life Contingencies
paras: An advanced course on problems of single lives and on the death and survival of multiple lives. 3 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 337
courses.title: Advanced Mechanics
paras: Vectorial treatment of physical problems Special examples from three-dimensional statics and dynamics. Introduction to the Lagrange equations.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 338
courses.title: Mathematical Statistics
paras: An advanced mathematical course including the multivariate normal law and related distributions. Normal regression theory. Applications to hypothesis testing and analysis of variance.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 339
courses.title: Electromagnetism
paras: I. Electrostatics and magnetostatics. The theorem of Gauss. Development of the Maxwell equations. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 425

courses.label: MATH 426
courses.title: Point Set Topology
paras: Topological spaces, Cartesian products, continuous mappings, separation axioms, connectedness, compact and locally compact spaces, metrizability.
1 hour per week.

courses.label: MATH 430
courses.title: Finite Projective Geometries
paras: Representations by fields, groups, and algebras. Finite Euclidean geometries. Sub-geometries. Collineation groups. Tactical configurations.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 431
courses.title: Algebra II
paras: A continuation of course 331. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 432
courses.title: Functions of 2 Complex Variable
paras: Topological concepts. Analytic continuation. The Riemann surface. Entire meromorphic functions. Periodic functions. Special functions. General metric spaces. Function spaces. The integral as an operator.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 433
courses.title: Metric Spaces and Integration
paras: Theory of metric spaces, completeness and compactness, measure in Euclidean n-space, the Lebesque integral, convergence theorems, the Fubini theorem, differentiability, absolute continuity.
1 hour per week.

courses.label: MATH 434
courses.title: Differential Equations of Mathematical Physics
paras: Boundary-value problems. Orthogonal functions. Bessel functions. The Legendre polynomials. The Fourier integral. The Laplace transform. The wave equation. ©
2 lectures, 1 hour problems.

courses.label: MATH 435
courses.title: Laboratory
paras: Numerical problems arising in actuarial science and statistics. 2 hours laboratory.

courses.label: MATH 436
courses.title: Mathematical Logic
paras: An informal introduction to the logic of sentences and predicates, with emphasis on analogies with familiar mathematical structures. Syllogisms and the algebra of sets related to predicate logic. Simplification, logical deduction, duality, consistency and completeness. The concepts of constant, variable, function, and set. Axiomatics.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 437
courses.title: Graduation and Mortality
paras: Methods of constructing and graduating mortality tables. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 438
courses.title: Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
paras: The mathematics and logic of estimation and hypothesis testing. Information. Consistency. Efficiency. Sufficiency. Fiducial and confidence intervals. The problems of large and small samples. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 439
courses.title: Theory of Experimental Design
paras: The logic of experimental designs. Randomization. Experimental and sampling errors. Mathematical methods of constructing various designs. Applications to problems in the sciences.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 440
courses.title: Advanced Probability
paras: Recurrent events. Markov processes and applications to Physics and Biology, including diffusion processes and epidemics. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 441
courses.title: Quantum Theory
paras: The classical mechanics of Lagrange and Hamilton. Introduction to quantum theory. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 442
courses.title: Theory of Relativity
paras: Covariant and contravariant tensors. Riemannian space. Gaussian curvature. The Lorentz transformation and Einstein’s special theory. Introduction to the general theory of relativity.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 443
courses.title: Electromagnetism II
paras: Applications of the Maxwell equations. Reflection and refraction. Introduction to wave guides and antennae. 2 lectures.
444, Elasticity. Problems in stress and strain. Isotropic bodies. Equilibrium equations. Torsion and flexure. 2 lectures.
445, Hydrodynamics. Continuous and discontinuous flow. Aerofoil theory. Viscous flow. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 446
courses.title: History of Mathematics
paras: The development of Mathematics from ancient to modern times, including study of prominent mathematicians and their works. Problems will be worked using both modern and historical approaches. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 447
courses.title: Statistical Mechanics
paras: Applications of probability theory to theoretical Physics. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 448
courses.title: Differential Geometry
paras: Curves in space. Gaussian curvature. Tensorial notation. Introduction to differential manifolds. 2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 449
courses.title: Experimental Design
paras: Logic of experimental designs. Randomization. Experimental and sampling errors. Designs applied in biology. Methods of analysis for factorial designs, Latin squares, etc.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 450
courses.title: Applied Analysis
paras: Applied Mathematics for Science majors. Ordinary and partial differential equations. Laplace and Fourier transforms. Special functions. Fourier series. Vector and matric methods. Calculus of variations. Other topics in advanced calculus.
2 lectures.

courses.label: MATH 601
courses.title: Advanced Numerical Analysis
paras: Finite differences, with stress on operator methods and central difference notation. Iterative procedures for solution of equations. Computations involving integrals. Error estimation. Curve fitting and orthogonal polynomials. Gaussian quadrature. Methods of solving ordinary and partial differential equations. Eigenvalue problems for systems of linear equations and for differential equations. Matric methods in applied mathematics.

courses.label: MATH 603
courses.title: Gas Dynamics
paras: Concepts from thermodynamics. One-dimensional gas dynamics. One-dimensional wave motion. Waves in supersonic flow. Flow in ducts and wind tunnels. Methods of measurement. Equations of frictionless flow. Small-perturbation theory. Bodies of revolution and slender body theory. The similarity rules of high-speed flow. Transonic flow. The method of characteristics. Effects of viscosity and conductivity. Laminar and turbulent boundary layers. Concepts from gas kinetics.

courses.label: MATH 604
courses.title: Special Functions
paras: Elliptic functions. The hypergeometric function. The gamma and beta functions. The functions of Laplace, Legendre, Lamé, Mathieu, and Bessel. Orthogonal functions; the functions of Laguerre, Hermite, Chebyshev.

courses.label: MATH 611
courses.title: Advanced Probability
paras: Review of classical probability theory, including occupancy problems, the binomial, Poisson, and nomal distributions, applications in physics. Recurrent events. Markov chains, stochastic processes, including the ruin problem and diffusion processes; application to information theory, radar, queuing problems, etc.

courses.label: MATH 621
courses.title: Computer Programming
paras: General concepts of computer types and applications. Flow charting. Coding, instruction formats. Editing. Storage elements and buffers. Control and accuracy in digital computers. Input and output devices and their use. Number systems. Automatic programming and universal computer languages. Logic and Boolean Algebra. Heuristic programming. Elements of logical design.

courses.label: MATH 622
courses.title: Vector and Tensor Analysis
paras: Vector spaces, linear transformations, matrices. Euclidean spaces, groups of transformations, algebra of tensors; covariant differentiation, divergence, Laplacian, curl. Generalizations to Riemannian spaces. Applications to other fields including differential geometry, mechanics, elasticity, hydrodynamics, electricity, and general relativity.

courses.label: MATH 631
courses.title: Advanced Computer Techniques
paras: Non-numeric computing. List processors and their application to the calculation of recursive functions, language translation, analytic differentiation and integration, mathematical logic, sorting, heuristic programming. Polish strings. Simulation of a List Processor.

courses.label: MATH 641
courses.title: Mathematical Methods for Operations Research
paras: Construction and analysis of mathematical models of systems and processes connected with Science and Engineering. Related topics in numerical methods, probability, statistics, and linear graph theory. Special methods such as simulation, queuing theory and: renewal theory. Methods of optimization including linear and non-linear programming, steepest descent, dynamic programming, and game theory.

courses.label: MATH 663
courses.title: Mathematical Logic
paras: 664, Calculus of Variations. The Euler equations and the Legendre and Jacobi conditions. The Weierstrass E function and sufficient conditions. The theory of transversals and isoperimetric problems. Hilbert’s existence theorem. Selected topics from the theories of Kneser and Caratheodory; the problem of Bolza.

courses.label: MATH 675
courses.title: Linear Graphs
paras: Definitions and basic theorems. Planar graphs and Kuratowski’s theorem. Selected topics from advanced graph theory.

courses.label: ME 13
courses.title: Kinematics
paras: A basic course in kinematics emphasizing the creative approach. Uniform rotary motion including rolling cylinders, gears and the synthesis of gear trains including planetaries. Non-uniform motion including cams, gears and linkages. Programming non-uniform motion and the synthesis of cam mechanisms, non-circular gear trains and linkages.
3 lectures, 3 hours laboratory, one term.

courses.label: ME 21
courses.title: Mechanics of Machinery
paras: The effects of dynamic forces in machines. Introduction to mechanical vibrations. Transient forces. Static force analysis, dynamic force analysis, balancing, cam dynamics, dynamics of feedback systems. Prerequisite: ME 13.
2 lectures, 3 hours laboratory, one term.

courses.label: ME 22
courses.title: Design of Machines
paras: Theory and application of mechanics of solids to machine parts. Design of machine elements; power screws, shafting, bearings, belts, gears, flywheels, clutches and brakes, crankshafts, springs, lubrication, ball and roller bearings.
Prerequisite: ME 21.
2 lectures, 2 hours laboratory, one term.

courses.label: ME 23
courses.title: Analysis and Synthesis of Machines
paras: Principle of optimum design, optimizing for minimum cost, maximum power capability, minimum weight, effects of manufacturing errors on product performance, statistical consideration for the factor of safety, optimum design of machine elements; torsion shafts, beams, gears, etc. Fluctuating loads, impact forces. Analog methods. Prerequisite: ME 22.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 25
courses.title: Mechanical Vibrations
paras: A broad development of mechanical vibration and impact. Transient phenomena, self-excited vibration, torsional oscillations, multi-mass systems, electromechanical systems and analogies. Forced vibrations, elimination and absorption of vibration. Measurement of vibration. Prerequisite: ME 21. .
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 35
courses.title: Nuclear Engineering
paras: An introductory course in nuclear reactor theory and design, isotope applications and fusion. Topics covered will include fission and the chain reaction, reactor principles, reactor components and materials, heat transfer, reactor design, uses of isotopes, applications of nuclear power and the fusion process. Radiation hazards and shielding.
Prerequisites: Math 31, Phys 15.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 36
courses.title: Physical Metallurgy
paras: Review of atomic and crystal structures. Theory of solidification of metals. Elasticity and plasticity of metals. Corrosion and diffusion. Properties of engineering alloys.
Prerequisites: Chem 11, Phys 15.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 37
courses.title: Ceramics
paras: The crystallography of ionic and co-valent compounds. A study of the mechanical properties of single crystals and polycrystals. Properties of special ceramic materials.
Prerequisites: Chem 11, Phys 15.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 42
courses.title: Industrial Economic Organization
paras: The economics and decision processes utilized in choosing between engineering alternatives and in choosing optimum operating levels. The topics discussed are costs, methods for tangible evaluation of alternatives, capital management, determination of minimum cost and maximum profit, risk, uncertainty and intangibles, elements of industrial measurement, analysis and forecasting.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 53
courses.title: Heat Transfer I
paras: Introduction to heat transfer mechanisms. The formulation of heat transfer problems. Temperature distributions in solids under steady and transient heat conduction. Laminar forced convection, the use of boundary layer theory and the integral method for evaluating the heat transfer coefficient. Laminar and turbulent free convection, empirical correlations and introductory analysis. Reynolds and Colburn analogies.
3 lectures, 3 hours laboratory, alternate weeks, one term.

courses.label: ME 54
courses.title: Thermodynamics II
paras: Review of the basic concepts and postulates of thermodynamics and the conditions for equilibrium. Reactive systems. An introduction to irreversible thermodynamics. Applications to selected engineering systems including direct conversion devices, gas turbines.
Prerequisite: GE 31.
3 lectures, 3 hours laboratory, one term.

3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 56
courses.title: Heat Transfer II
paras: Forced convection in high-speed flow. Boiling and condensation. Ablation. Mass transfer in laminar and turbulent flows, empirical correlations and an introduction to analysis by the boundary-layer theory and by the integral approach. Radiation heat transfer, radiative properties, geometrical factors, analogue methods. Simple kinetic theory of transport properties.
Prerequisite: ME 53.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 62
courses.title: Fluid Dynamics
paras: Fundamental concepts of fluid flow: vorticity, circulation, stream function and velocity potential. Integral formulation of the governing laws of fluid dynamics. Combination of uniform flow with flows generated by singularities. Two and three dimensional ideal flow over simple bodies. Introduction to conformal mapping principles.
Prerequisite: GE 32, Math 44.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 63
courses.title: Turbomachines
paras: Performance characteristics of turbomachines, similarity laws. The physics of cavitation, cavitation inception characteristics. Mach number effects. Momentum and energy relations for fluid masses, energy transfer in turbomachines. Cascade mechanics, application of thin aerofoil theory to blade design. Three-dimensional effects, actuator disk theory. Boundary layer behaviour in turbomachines.
Prerequisite: GE 32.
3 lectures, 3 hours laboratory, one term.

courses.label: ME 64
courses.title: Hydraulic Engineering
paras: Descriptive and quantitative analyses in hydrology. Elements of hydraulic projects, reservoirs, dams, pipe lines, open channel flow; water hammer. Machinery of hydraulic projects. Hydraulic power plants. Economic aspects of hydraulic engineering projects.
Prerequisite: GE 32.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 65
courses.title: Gasdynamics
paras: Foundations of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics. The introductory concepts of compressible fluid flow. Isentropic flow behaviour; normal and oblique shock waves. Flow in constant area ducts with friction and heat transfer. Generalized one-dimensional continuous flow. Prerequisites: ME 53, GE 32.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 66
courses.title: Turbulent Flow I
paras: Reynolds stresses, intensity and scale of turbulence. The “law of the wall”, logarithmic velocity profile and velocity defect laws, effects of roughness. Pressure loss in pipes and conduits, skin friction in boundary layers, determination of profile drag. Free turbulence, jets and wakes. Atmospheric turbulence, effects of density stratification.
Prerequisites: GE 32, Math 51.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 73
courses.title: Human Factors Engineering
paras: The problems of incorporating human beings into engineering systems. The topics discussed are: the human visual, auditory and musculo-skeletal system, multiple sensory inputs, man-machine dynamics, environmental factors, human stress, group dynamics, and workplace design; the evaluation and testing of man-machine systems.
3 lectures, one term.

courses.label: ME 81
courses.title: Seminar
paras: Designed to give the student personal experience in oral presentation of technical information. Also provides an opportunity for students to attend seminars on topics of interest presented by recognized workers in the field.
1 hour, one term.

courses.label: ME 82
courses.title: Mechanical Engineering Projects
paras: Engineering assignments requiring the student to demonstrate initiative and assume responsibility. Student activity is guided and co-ordinated by faculty supervisors. In selecting and assigning projects, particular account is taken of the student’s field of specialization. Projects, in general, involve technical disciplines beyond the strictly mechanical engineering field.
9 hours laboratory, one term.
Graduate and Research Programmes

In a field of applied science such as Mechanical Engineering the heart of any graduate work involves a thesis project with substantial experimental content. The freshly registered graduate student interviews several faculty members active in research in a field of possible interest to him and chooses a thesis project with the concurrence of some faculty member who will then act as his supervisor. Normally such a faculty member also arranges financial support for the graduate student with the aid of externally obtained research grants. For this reason it is difficult to arrange such financial support before the student’s arrival on the campus. The choice of the thesis project is an important decision, because a later change in the student’s field of research usually entails loss of time. Active fields of research in which students may at present be accepted are listed and described in the following section. It must be kept in mind, however, that the list is only intended as a guide since new topics are added frequently as the sphere of interest of the faculty expands, while some projects are completed or abandoned.
Once a thesis project has been chosen, a suitable programme of course work to support the research work is agreed upon between the student and the super-
Department of Mechanical Engineering
visor. When approved by the Faculty of Graduate Studies, this programme together with the thesis project constitutes the official set of requirements for obtaining the degree sought by the student.
Active Research Projects
Materials Science.

In one project a plasma torch is used, which is an electric discharge maintained in a controlled atmosphere, in this case of Argon gas. Very high temperatures (up to 30,000°C) may be maintained in the plasma torch with the aid of which, in the precisely controlled atmosphere surrounding the torch, single crystals of ceramic materials may be induced to grow.

Another research project is aimed at investigating the influence of dislocation interactions on apparent work hardening rates in single crystalline solids. A number of experimental techniques are employed to produce slip in pre-determined orientations thereby permitting an analysis of the dislocation intersections and interactions which occur upon deformation.
Design Studies.

The Design Studies Group is supported by the University, the National Design Council and interested industries. It has the purpose of investigating the various aspects of industrial design and the problems of the individual industrial designer. The area of primary concern to the group at the present time is the organizational structure surrounding the industrial designer and how it affects his level of performance.
Fluid Power Control Systems.

One active project in this area is a theoretical and experimental investigation of a hydraulic control spool valve. The flow of hydraulic fluid through a spooltype valve may be highly unstable, resulting in erratic operation of the system in which it is the chief control element. It is the purpose of the investigation to study the flow and to determine methods by which the instability may be alleviated.
Other projects planned in this area include an experimental investigation of a fluid jet control valve and of a submerged jet impinging normally on an eccentric orifice.
Aero-Space Propulsion.

Three projects are under way in the general area of aero-space propulsion. One is a study of the formation of oxide smokes in the combustion of metals. Another is an investigation of the combustion of liquid fuels at pressures near the critical. The third project is the design and construction of a simulator to reproduce some of the phenomena associated with flow in solid-propellant rocket motors.
In the first project flame spectroscopy is used in an attempt to discover the vapour-phase reactions taking place when metals burn.

Transient effects become important in the combusion of liquid fuels at high pressures when the density of vapourized fuel is of the same order as that of the liquid. Time-resolved spectroscopy and high-speed motion pictures are used to study the unsteady effects in these flames.

The solid-propellant simulator is being designed for the study of flow phenomena in rocket motors. In particular, it is of interest to examine the relationship between the stability of the gas flow and the boundary conditions imposed on the flow field by the burning charge.
Ground Effect Machines.

The purpose of this research program is to investigate the influence of ground effects on the aerodynamic characteristics of very low aspect ratio lifting surfaces. The lifting surface envisaged is a ram wing type Ground Effect Machine in which pneumatic side jets and a trailing edge jet are used to contain the pressure field generated on the lower surface. This concept fits into the general category of vehicles known as hovercraft or Ground Effect Machines (GEMS).
Air Pollution.
One project is entitled “Atmospheric Dispersal of Heavy Particles” and is concerned with the rate of spread of dust clouds emitted from chimneys. In the
Department of Mechanical Engineering

experimental work, glass microspheres are blown into the atmosphere at the top of a 60 foot mast and collected on adhesive tape exposed in a grid pattern surrounding the mast. The glass spheres can be identified under a microscope and counted. Another project is concerned with the rise of a hot smoke plume: owing to their buoyancy, hot gases from a chimney rise to some height before dispersing.
Work on the Great Lakes.
Turbulence and Diffusion. Fluorescent dye released at a point-source may be detected in very low concentrations and enables a study of mixing processes to be made.

Internal waves. During summer the lakes become stratified, a warm, relatively light surface layer lying on top of a colder and heavier mass below. The interface, the “thermocline”, behaves much like a free surface (air/water interface) in that wave motions may be observed on it.

Lake currents. Winds and atmospheric pressure disturbances produce a variety of complicated current patterns. These are investigated using “drogues”, i.e., two metal sheets. assembled at 90° so as to offer a high drag and attached to small surface floats.
Graduate Course Descriptions

601, Aerodynamics of Compressible Fluids. Two-dimensional subsonic flow with small perturbations; hodograph and other methods of solution. Threedimensional subsonic flow. Two-dimensional supersonic flow with small perturbations; the method of characteristics. Oblique shocks. Axially symmetric supersonic flow. Supersonic wing theory. Hypersonic flow.
One term.

courses.label: ME 605
courses.title: Kinematics II
paras: An extension of ME 13. Computing mechanisms, space mechanisms. Use of computers in synthesis and analysis. Four-bar linkage, coupler curves, path curvature. Euler-Savory equation, polode curvature. Numerical and graphical methods. Five-bar linkages.
One term.

courses.label: ME 606
courses.title: Hypersonic Aerodynamics
paras: Fundamental concepts of hypersonic flow. Two- and three-dimensional hypersonic flow. Hypersonic small-disturbance theory. Slender body theory. Minimum drag bodies. Hypersonic flow over blunt bodies. Stability and control of hypersonic vehicles. Real gas effects. One term.

courses.label: ME 615
courses.title: Fundamentals of Aerodynamic Heating
paras: Basic equations and properties of laminar and turbulent boundary layers. Skin friction and heat transfer. Predictions by approximate methods. Basic parameter for low density flow. Slip and free-molecule fiow. Stagnation point heat transfer. Mass transfer cooling.
One term.

courses.label: ME 621
courses.title: Survey of Space Technology
paras: Brief survey of propulsion, celestial mechanics, astronomy and astrophysics of the solar system. Energy conversion in space. Electric propulsion and fundamentals of magnetohydrodynamics. Reentry dynamics, ablative heat protection, trajectory analysis. Optimum thrust and steering programmes. Lunar trip. Summary of experimental results on geophysics, cosmic radiation, the earth’s atmosphere. Materials for space. One term.

courses.label: ME 625
courses.title: Experimental Mechanics
paras: Classification and estimation of errors. Smoothing of experimental data. Similitude and model laws. Analogue methods in experimental stress analysis. Electrical and mechanical strain gauges, transducers. Brittle coatings. Photoelasticity.
One term.

courses.label: ME 631
courses.title: Fluid Power Control
paras: Fundamentals of fluid flow. Fluid power conversion in positive displacement. Pumps and motors, performance characteristics. Energy storage in working fluids, unsteady flow with elastic-energy storage. Fluid power transmission: dynamic response characteristics. Hydraulic and pneumatic control valve configurations. Dynamic interaction in hydraulic, pneumatic and electric control systems. Valve instability and non-linear effects in hydraulic systems with inertia loading.
One term.

courses.label: ME 641
courses.title: Theory of Metallic Materials
paras: Bond theory, Fermi levels, dia-para and ferro-magnetism. Theoretical and experimental studies of dislocations. Structure and behaviour of polycrystalline metals.
One term.

courses.label: ME 642
courses.title: Behaviour of Materials
paras: Review of basic crystallography. Dislocation theory with special reference to non-metallic substances. Properties and influence of point defects. Ductility, fatigue and fracture phenomena. Surface effects. Mechanical properties of special single crystal polycrystals and polyphase materials.
One term.

courses.label: ME 643
courses.title: Technology of Manufacture
paras: The classical theory of plasticity, with particular reference to forming processes. Elements of tensors, stress, strain, yield and flow; strain-hardening, anisotropy, experimental evidence. Extremum principles, slip line fields, limit analysis. Forging, impact forging, drawing, extrusion, sheet and tube forming, rolling. Instability. Speed and temperature effects. Approximate technological theories; residual stress. Cutting, milling and grinding.
One term.

courses.label: ME 651
courses.title: Conduction Heat Transfer
paras: Steady and transient heat conduction in isotropic media. Conduction in flowing media. Conduction in stagnant films with mass transfer. Heat conduction with phase change and moving boundaries. Problems of heat conduction in anisotropic media.
Prerequisite: ME 53.
One term.
Department of Mechanical Engineering

courses.label: ME 652
courses.title: Radiation Heat Transfer I
paras: Fundamentals of radiation. Determination of radiation properties. Analysis of radiation heat transfer. Solar, terrestrial and planetary radiation. Temperature control of satellites and space vehicles. Solar power plants for space vehicles. Direct solar energy conversion systems.
One term.

courses.label: ME 653
courses.title: Radiation Heat Transfer II
paras: Summary of radiation between surfaces, view factors, emissivity measurements. Flame radiation, radiation from clouds of luminous particles. Gas radiation, calculation of flame emissivities based on flame spectroscopy. Optical temperature measurement.
One term.

courses.label: ME 654
courses.title: Transport Phenomena
paras: A survey of the equations of heat, mass, and momentum transfer in a fluid. Examples of similarity. Evaluation of transport properties, kinetic theory of ideal gases, Chapman-Enskog theory, introduction to kinetic theory of liquids. Transport properties in turbulent flow. Introductory kinetics of evaporation and condensation. The transport of small particles of condensed phase in a fluid. Radiative energy transport, the absorption of radiation in a fluid.
One term.

courses.label: ME 655
courses.title: Combustion
paras: Review of combustion thermodynamics. Combustion of premixed gases, detonations. Laminar and turbulent diffusion flames. Combustion in flow systems, flame holders. Heterogeneous combustion, solid fuels, liquid droplets. Combustion of metals. Ignition and flame spread. Applications of the theories to furnaces, gas turbines, reciprocating I-C engines, and rocket motors.
Prerequisite: ME 654.
One term.

courses.label: ME 661
courses.title: Mechanics of Ideal Fluid Flow
paras: General equations of ideal fluid flow. Persistence of circulation, method of images, distributed sources. Twodimensional potential fiow. Conformal mapping transformation, complex potential. Superposition principle. Free streamlines, Schwarz-Christoffel transformation, Blasius Theorem, vortex flow, Helmholtz Theorem, Munk’s vortexsheet theory.
One term.

courses.label: ME 662
courses.title: Viscous Flow
paras: Stress tensor, rate of strain tensor, Navier-Stokes equations. Some exact solutions. Creeping Flow. Boundary Layer equations. Falkner- Skan similarity solutions. Momentum and energy integral equations, approximate methods. Effects of buoyancy, heat transfer and compressibility. Threedimensional boundary layers. Stability of laminar flow, the origin of turbulence.
Prerequisite: GE 32.
One term.

courses.label: ME 664
courses.title: Turbulent Flow II
paras: Stochastic averages, methods of measurement of fluctuating quantities. Homogeneous turbulence models, velocity correlations and spectra, energy dissipation. Kolmogoroff’s theory of local isotropy. The structure of turbulence in shear flow, intermittency. Transport phenomena in

turbulent flow, “absolute” and “relative” diffusion, effects of scale. Applications to pipe and boundary layer flow, jets, wakes, atmospheric and oceanic turbulence. The generation of aerodynamic noise in shear layers and boundary layers.
Prerequisite: ME 66.
One term.

courses.label: ME 666
courses.title: Wave Phenomena in Fluid Flow
paras: Fundamental concepts of fluid flow and wave motion. The equation of wave motion and list of solutions. Water waves: Theory of tidal waves, surface waves and capillary waves. Inertial and elastic waves: inertance, capacitance, impedance of pipes, waterhammer equations, surge effects. Plane and spherical acoustic waves, near and far field equations, wave propagation in stratified media, blast waves in atmosphere and underwater, dynamic blast loads. Prerequisite: ME 62
GE 31
One term.

courses.label: PHIL 100
courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy
paras: The normal first course in Philosophy both for those intending to proceed further and for those desiring a single terminal course. The student will attempt to come to grips with some of the fundamental problems of human life, for example, those associated with the nature of matter, mind, reality, knowledge, religion, virtue and beauty. Philosophies both ancient and modern will be discussed and some time devoted to the consideration of the structure of inference (logic) as it occurs in science and other instances of reasoning, argument, proof, and persuasion.
3 hours.
1003. Introduction to Philosophy. A study of St. Thomas and his writings; fundamental Thomistic principles.
3 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 140J
courses.title: Logic and Epistemology
paras: Nature and division of Philosophy; nature of logic, the term; the proposition; argumentation; induction and deduction; scientific demonstration. Truth; certitude; evidence; sense and intellectual knowledge; criterion of truth; contemporary theories.
3 hours.

2003. Cosmology and Philosophy of Science. Corporeal bodies and change; quantitative and qualitative characteristics; motion; time, space; hylomorphic theory. Nature of science; abstraction; necessity; foundation and object of science; scientific method; hypothesis and theory.
3 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 201
courses.title: Ethics and Value Theory
paras: The philosophical approach to the fundamental questions about human values as they affect contemporary. problems. Important ethical and political positions of past and present will be examined. Emphasis will be placed on the relevance of ethics to the study of human behaviour within the framework of the social sciences. Recommended as the normal Philosophy course following on from Philosophy 100 for those students who do not intend to pursue the 260-261-360 sequence. The first half of this course (designated as 201a) may be taken by students from other faculties who require a one-semester course.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100 is recommended.
3 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 220
courses.title: Logic
paras: Rigorous and systematic treatment of truth-functional and quantificational theory, with some treatment also devoted to semantical and metalinguistic theory, proof theory, the foundations of mathematics, inductive logic, and non-extensional systems.

Philosophy 220 gives the student ample preparation for further work in mathematical logic, philosophical analysis, and the philosophy of science. It should also prove very useful for those doing work in linguistics.
Prerequisite: None.
3 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 240J
courses.title: Ethics
paras: End of Man; the human act; law, conscience; morality; rights and duties; duties of a man as an individual and as a member of society. 3 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 250
courses.title: Tutorial for Honours
paras: 1 hour.

courses.label: PHIL 260A
courses.title: History of Philosophy I
paras: A preliminary examination of the philosophy of Plato. Mention will be made of the historical Socrates and some of the Presocratics.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 260B
courses.title: History of Philosophy II
paras: A preliminary account of early modern philosophies, with emphasis on the views of Descartes, Locke, Malebranche, Leibniz, Spinoza, Berkeley, Hume.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 261A
courses.title: Moral Philosophy
paras: The various alternative ways of dealing theoretically with questions about human moral value. Views of some of the following positions will be discussed: the Epicureans, the Stoics, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Christianity, Spinoza, the Utilitarians, Nietzsche, Schopenhauer, Shaftesbury. Emphasis will be placed on relating these various views to the ethical pronouncements of the modern social sciences particularly cultural anthropology, behaviourism and Freud.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
3 hours, half course.
Department of Philosophy

courses.label: PHIL 261B
courses.title: History of Philosophy HI. A preliminary examination of the philosophy of Aristotle, particularly with reference to his metaphysics, physics and psychology, a preliminary examination of Mediaeval philosophy. Prerequisite: Philosophy 100
paras: 3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 260–261
courses.title: Note: This series of four half-courses will be offered each year. In
paras: 261 the order of the a and b half course is reversible. These courses are intended primarily for second year honours students, and for others willing and able to go rather thoroughly into the matters concerned.

courses.label: PHIL 300J
courses.title: Metaphysics and Natural Theology
paras: The notion and analogy of being; the primary principles of being; the properties, division, and causes of being. Demonstration of existence of God; His nature and attributes; the divine intelligence and will; creation and providence.
3 hours.

301a, Modern Ethics I. Discussion of the moral philosophies of some recent philosophers. Samples of the work of British, American, and Continental philosophers will be analysed. Some attempt will be made to acquaint students with the work of philosophers of a number of schools.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 301B
courses.title: Modern Ethics II
paras: Contemporary ethical problems. Exploration of the epistemological and logical foundations of current ethical issues and discussion of specific problems such as the analysis of moral concepts, the significance and nature of the problem of free will, the data of ethics, the nature of moral rules and the bearing upon ethics of such problems as immortality and the existence of God.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 315
courses.title: Political Philosophy
paras: Philosophical analysis of central concepts in political theory. The effect of the central issues of moral philosophy, epistemology, and metaphysics on the formation of political theories. Examples will be drawn from the work of philosophers of a number of periods and schools — for example, Plato, Aristotle, St. Thomas Aquinas, Hobbes, Locke, Hegel, Marx and contemporary thinkers.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 320
courses.title: Aesthetics
paras: The philosophical consideration of art and beauty. A study of the basic problems with examples from historical and contemporary writers. Various theories of art criticism and literary criticism. Art related to society, morality, the sciences and religion. . Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 330A
courses.title: Oriental Philosophy
paras: A survey of non-western philosophy, particularly that of China, Japan, and India. The views of such philosophers as Confucius, Lao-Tze and Mencius will be discussed and the philosophical content of the early Hindu and Buddhist writings examined. Zen Buddhism and other modern views.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 330B
courses.title: Philosophy of History
paras: Consideration of the various possible views about the ultimate nature and significance of history and historical knowledge. The views of such as the following are examined: St. Augustine, Vico, Hegel, Marx, Spengler, Croce, Collingwood and Toynbee.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 330C
courses.title: Philosophy of Religion
paras: A philosophical approach to the basic ideas of great world religions. The phenomenology of religious experience and mysticism and the nature of religious symbolism and language will be discussed. Enquiry will also be made into such characteristically religious notions as faith and revelation, sin and redemption.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100.
3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 330D
courses.title: Special Subject in Philosophy
paras: The instructor presents a theme of special interest to himself well within the grasp of general students who have taken an introductory philosophy course.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 100 or 15.
3 hours, half course.

courses.label: PHIL 340
courses.title: Interdisciplinary Seminar
paras: Specific problems regarding the philosophical underpinnings of various sciences and disciplines, including Physics, Biology, Mathematics, Psychology, History, Political Science and Economics, English and other literatures. 2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 340J
courses.title: History of Philosophy
paras: A survey of Philosophy from Presocratics to contemporary philosophers.

courses.label: PHIL 348J
courses.title: Seminar in Philosophy
paras: A special study of the principal philosophers of the modern and contemporary eras. 3 hours.

paras: For Philosophy majors in the pass course. 1 hour.

courses.label: PHIL 360
courses.title: History of Philosophy IV-V. The Philosophy of Kant, his predecessors and successors
paras: Considerations of Rationalism and Empiricism not dealt with in Philosophy 260b, particularly those which are specially relevant to the Critical Philosophy. The Critique of Pure Reason. A survey of post-Kantian idealism with emphasis on Hegel.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 260.
3 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 375
courses.title: Philosophy of Science
paras: Thorough introduction to the philosophical issues bearing specifically upon, or arising out of, science. Logical analysis of scientific methods and concepts, study of the role of mathematics in empirical science, consideration of the relations among the various sciences and between the “theoretical” and “applied” branches of particular sciences, and comparison of science as an activity with art, religion, philosophy and everyday life. Some attention will also be devoted to special problems arising from the social sciences, especially psychology.

Prerequisite: Philosophy 220. Very moderate acquaintance with the sciences is assumed. Well-qualified students in the sciences, however, may be admitted without Philosophy 220. May be taken concurrently with 220.
3 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 375A
courses.title: The first semester of the Philosophy of Science course may be taken separately by students in Engineering and others requiring a half-course
paras: Effort will be made to ensure that this portion of the course does not explicitly presuppose Philosophy 220.

courses.label: PHIL 450
courses.title: Epistemology
paras: The basic problems in the theory of knowledge, the nature of logieal inference, concepts, causal and rational necessity, determinism, freedom, meaning, language, the fundamental nature of communication. Prerequisite: Philosophy 360.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 452
courses.title: Ancient Philosophy
paras: Detailed consideration of selected portions of the works of Plato and Aristotle, Suggested Works: Plato’s Timaeus, Theaetetus and Philebus. Aristotle’s Metaphysics.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 260, 261.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 453
courses.title: Mediaeval Philosophy
paras: Detailed consideration of selected portions of the works of St. Thomas and other Mediaeval philosophers such as Occam, St. Anselm, Albertus Magnus, St. Bernard, Duns Scotus.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 260, 261.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 454
courses.title: Continental Rationalism
paras: The Philosophy of Descartes, Leibniz and Spinoza.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 360.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 456
courses.title: Existential Philosophy and Phenomenology
paras: A study of selected readings. Prerequisite: Philosophy 360. With the consent of the instructor, this course is also open to general students with two full courses in Philosophy.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 457
courses.title: Metaphysics
paras: Theories of reality including study of such fundamental concepts as being, form, substance, causality, process, universal and particular. Prerequisite: Philosophy 360.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 458
courses.title: Analytic Philosophy
paras: Introduction to the rigorous and detailed philosophizing of the contemporary era. Readings from such figures as Frege, Russell, Moore, Lewis, Ayer, Carnap, Quine, Ryle, Austin, and especially Ludwig Wittgenstein.
Prerequisite: Two courses in Philosophy. Philosophy 220 is specially recommended.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 460
courses.title: Problems
paras: Seminar projects not readily classifiable into the above categories.
Prerequisite: Philosophy 360.
2 hours..

courses.label: PHIL 470
courses.title: Tutorials for Honour Students in Special Subjects
paras: 1 hour.

courses.label: PHIL 480-9
courses.title: Selected Study of One Philosopher
paras: The intensive study of one significant figure in the History of Philosophy. 2 hours, half or full course.
499, Senior Honours Essay.
1 hour.

courses.label: PHIL 610-19
courses.title: Seminar in the Study of a Recent Philosopher
paras: Names at present contemplated from which a choice may be made should the demand be sufficient: Bradley, Heidegger, McTaggart, Price, Russell, Ryle, Sartre, Wittgenstein.
2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 620
courses.title: Seminar in Presocratic Philosophy
paras: The key ideas of Greek philosophy from Anaximander to the Atomists, their logical implications as well as their influence on later ages will be discussed. The foundation of philosophical thinking will be elucidated against the background of the mythological attitude that preceded it. Attention will also be given to early cosmological and anthropological speculation.
2 hours.

courses.title: Seminar in the Philosophy of Kant
paras: 2 hours.

courses.label: PHIL 622
courses.title: Seminar in the Philosophy of Hegel and Post-Kantian Idealism
paras: 2 hours.

courses.title: Specially Directed Studies
paras: 2 hours.

paras: 1 hour per week consultation.
